title: Nationwide Flight Groundings Spark $50 Billion Battle on Capitol Hill Over FAA Upgrades
snippet: Following a massive air traffic control breakdown that stranded travelers nationwide, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy is pushing Congress for a $50 billion emergency modernization package, triggering sharp resistance from lawmakers over unspent funds and an impending shutdown deadline.
content:
WASHINGTON — A crippling nationwide air traffic control outage last week has ignited a high-stakes funding showdown on Capitol Hill, as lawmakers grapple with how to overhaul the nation’s aging aviation system while racing to avoid a mid-December government shutdown.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy is aggressively lobbying Congress to fast-track an ambitious $50 billion package to modernize the Federal Aviation Administration's (FAA) telecommunications network. The emergency request follows a disastrous failure in the FAA's communications system sparked by a routine router replacement in El Dorado, Arkansas, where workers were swapping out legacy copper wiring for fiber-optic cable.

President Donald Trump framed the crisis as an inevitable outcome of decades of reliance on antique technology. "Essentially, what you saw on Friday was very, very old equipment that had a heart attack," Trump told reporters, expressing optimism that Congress would step up with fresh funding.

Bipartisan Resistance Hits the Hill

While lawmakers universally acknowledge that the FAA's technological backbone needs urgent modernization, Duffy’s $50 billion request has drawn sharp skepticism from both sides of the aisle.

Senate Republicans expressed confusion over how the administration's initial pitch of $30 billion jumped by another $20 billion almost overnight. Sen. John Kennedy, R-La., said officials "just need to do a better job of explaining it to us," while Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., underscored that Congress requires a thorough accounting of the figures before moving forward.

Democrats, meanwhile, pointed to existing funding that has yet to be touched. Rep. Eric Larsen, D-Wash., top Democrat on the House Transportation Committee, noted that $11 billion of a previously approved $12.5 billion allocation remains unspent. Rep. Rosa DeLauro, D-Conn., the ranking Democrat on the House Appropriations Committee, blasted the request as a "$50 billion ransom without a real plan to deliver."

Looming Shutdown Deadline Heightens Stakes

Duffy has pushed back against critics, asserting that existing radar systems date back to the 1960s and critical infrastructure still relies on tech from the 1990s. He emphasized that previously allocated funds were tightly restricted by Congress and could not be repurposed to construct the modern telecommunications network the country desperately needs.

The fight over air safety funding comes at a sensitive moment for Capitol Hill negotiations, with lawmakers facing a Dec. 11 deadline to keep the federal government funded. Department of Transportation officials are slated to brief congressional committees this week to make their case.
